name: A Survey of Self-Evolving Agents: On Path to Artificial Super Intelligence (full subtitle: What, When, How, and Where to Evolve on the Path to Artificial Super Intelligence)
authors: Huan-ang Gao, Jiayi Geng, Wenyue Hua, Mengkang Hu, Xinzhe Juan et al. (27 authors); lead/corresponding affiliations: Princeton University & Princeton AI Lab (Mengdi Wang), with Tsinghua, CUHK, UIUC, PSU, SJTU and others
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 01/2026 (arXiv preprint 2507.21046, first submitted Jul 2025)
code_url: https://github.com/CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents (curated paper/resource list, not a single executable method)
reflection_type: none (survey/roadmap that taxonomizes reflection mechanisms rather than proposing one). The surveyed methods span verbal-self-critique (Reflexion, Self-Refine), tool/environment-verified, learned-critic / reward-model, search-guided (PromptAgent MCTS), multi-agent debate/collaboration, and population/evolutionary approaches; the survey itself contributes a unifying what/when/how/where framework.
feedback_source: n/a for the survey itself; it organizes the surveyed signal sources into: self-generated textual feedback, external tools (compiler/interpreter/web/search), unit-tests, environment-reward (scalar/verifiable), ground-truth/oracle labels, and human feedback. A core 'how to evolve' axis is textual feedback vs. scalar reward, and feedback source internal (model-generated) vs. external.
iteration_structure: n/a (survey). Catalogs the full spectrum: single-shot, iterative-refine (Self-Refine, TextGrad), episodic-retry (Reflexion), tree/MCTS search (PromptAgent), and population/evolutionary search (PromptBreeder, EvoAgent, ADAS). Temporally split into intra-test-time (online, within one task) and inter-test-time (offline/online, across tasks).
reflection_object: All of them — the survey's central 'what to evolve' dimension explicitly enumerates the objects of evolution: (1) Model/weights (the underlying LLM via SFT/RL), (2) Context = prompt/instructions + memory, (3) Tools (acquiring/creating/managing tools and skills), and (4) Architecture (single-agent workflow and multi-agent collaborative structure). It thus covers output content, reasoning chains, action trajectories, prompt/context, reusable skills/workflows, the agent's own code/architecture, and model weights.
requires_training: n/a (survey). It explicitly frames self-evolution across three learning paradigms it surveys: in-context learning (no weight update), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL, including online/on-policy and off-policy/DPO), plus nested meta-RL+SFT (e.g., self-edit/SEAL-style intra-test-time SFT driven by RL).
reward_or_critic_model: n/a for the survey; it categorizes the surveyed improvement signals into self-as-judge (Self-Refine, SPO pairwise self-preference), trained reward models / outcome-reward models (WebRL ORM), verifiable rewards (math/code), process- vs outcome-based reward granularity, and separate retrospective/critic or memory-manager models (e.g., Memory-R1 RL-trained memory manager).
distillation_target: All forms — the survey systematizes how reflection/experience is distilled into reusable artifacts: episodic-memory (long-term memory banks, Mem0, A-mem, Memento), reusable-skill/workflow (Agent Workflow Memory, Voyager-style skill library, MUSE hierarchical memory), structured-rules/insights (ExpeL rules, ReasoningBank reasoning strategies, ACE 'playbook' contexts), prompts (APE/ProTeGi/PromptBreeder/SPO), and model-weights (STaR, SELF, SEAL self-edits).
emergent_vs_engineered: Covers both. The survey discusses prompt/scaffold-engineered reflective behavior (Reflexion, Self-Refine, AdaPlanner) AND RL-emergent / weight-update self-improvement (STaR, SELF, SEAL self-edits, LADDER/TTRL test-time RL, WebRL self-evolving curriculum). A guiding thesis is the shift from scaffold-engineered in-context adaptation toward learned/parametric self-evolution on the path to ASI.
memory_type: n/a (survey). Surveys the full memory spectrum: short-term/scratchpad, long-term episodic memory banks, skill libraries, structured notes/knowledge graphs (A-mem Zettelkasten-style interconnected networks), and playbook/cheatsheet contexts (ACE). Memory is treated as a first-class 'what to evolve' component (Context = prompt + memory).
memory_persistence: n/a (survey). Explicitly spans within-episode (intra-test-time), cross-episode/cross-task (inter-test-time experience accumulation), and cross-session/lifelong (long-horizon lifelong-learning evaluation, persistent state across tasks without reset, e.g., EvoAgent's persistent experience pool + continual world model).
memory_curation_mechanism: n/a (survey) but it explicitly catalogs curation strategies: append-only experience logs; self-summarized/curated insights (MemInsight, ExpeL rules); retrieval-gated case banks (Memento); overwrite/evolution via self-relinking and structured ops ADD/MERGE/UPDATE/DELETE (Mem0, A-mem dynamic indexing/linking, Memory-R1 RL-trained manager); forgetting policies (SAGE Ebbinghaus curve, memory decay / right-to-be-forgotten unlearning); and population/Pareto-style selection for population-based methods.
error_localization_granularity: n/a (survey). Discusses signal granularity as an explicit axis: outcome-level (coarse, end-of-trajectory) vs process-level (fine, per-step) reward granularity; response/step/trajectory-level textual feedback; and agent-level attribution in multi-agent settings. It treats reward granularity (outcome-based vs process-based) as a key cross-cutting 'how to evolve' dimension.
intra_task_vs_inter_task: Covers both as the central 'when to evolve' dichotomy: intra-test-time self-evolution (adaptation during execution of a single task, coupled to the immediate instance, e.g., AdaPlanner, LADDER TTRL, SEAL self-edits) vs inter-test-time self-evolution (learning between tasks from accumulated experience, e.g., ExpeL, AWM, STaR, WebRL).
failure_recovery_vs_avoidance: n/a (survey) but covers all: mid-trajectory recovery (AdaPlanner out-of-plan replanning, TrustAgent rule-based in-flight revision), post-hoc revision (Self-Refine, TextGrad), and avoidance/retry-next-episode (Reflexion-style episodic retry, inter-test-time policy updates). It distills strategies from both successful and failed trajectories (ReasoningBank).
task_domains: Survey spans general-purpose and specialized domains. Explicitly: coding/autonomous software engineering, GUI/web navigation, math/reasoning, QA, tool-use, dialogue, decision-making, and specialized verticals — finance, medical/healthcare, education, plus embodied/games (Minecraft, Atari) and multi-agent collaboration.
benchmarks: Survey-level coverage of evaluation resources, including: ARC, WebArena, Mind2Web-Live, GAIA, SWE-bench (named in evaluation discussion), AUTOENV-36, MemoryAgentBench (Test-Time Learning dimension), LTMBenchmark, LifelongAgentBench, StuLife, Benchmark Self-Evolving, TRACE, and EvoAgent's 67-task Minecraft + Atari suite. Introduces evaluation paradigms: static, short-horizon adaptive, long-horizon lifelong-learning.
headline_result: No single headline number (survey). Illustrative figures it reports: EvoAgent improves overall Minecraft Success Rate from 21.80% to 30.29% (relative gain approx. 105.9%) under long-horizon lifelong-learning evaluation; an architecture/population-based design-search entry reaches 84.7 in the how-to-evolve overview table. The paper's primary contribution is the unified what/when/how/where-to-evolve taxonomy, not a benchmark SOTA.
baselines: n/a (survey). Positions itself as the first systematic survey of self-evolving agents; compares conceptually against related paradigms it distinguishes (curriculum learning, lifelong/continual learning, model editing, unlearning) and against prior narrower surveys on LLM agents, memory, or self-improvement.
gains_vs_baseline: n/a (survey provides no head-to-head gain of its own). It tabulates representative methods' reported gains as exemplars (e.g., EvoAgent overall SR 21.80%->30.29%, ~+105.9% relative; roughly doubled SR on Gold/Diamond Minecraft tiers vs baselines with >6x fewer ineffective steps and ~2.7 vs ~7 A100-days).
compute_cost_profile: n/a (survey) but it foregrounds compute as a cross-cutting concern: discusses online/offline and on-policy/off-policy trade-offs (off-policy improves sample efficiency at cost of distribution shift), test-time scaling/inference-time adaptation cost growing non-linearly with adaptation complexity, and proposes efficiency metrics such as Cost-per-Gain (CPG), tokens-per-success, memory growth rate, and training wall-clock (e.g., ~2.7 vs ~7 A100-days for EvoAgent).
known_limitations: As a survey it notes its own scope limits: a rapidly forming area with contested conceptual boundaries, framed as a 'guiding synthesis' rather than a review of an established paradigm; no rigid taxonomic boundaries. For the field it identifies open challenges: catastrophic forgetting / stability-plasticity dilemma, robust cross-domain knowledge transfer/generalization, scalability and non-linear compute cost, safety degradation during evolution ('misevolution'), reward hacking under off-policy learning, data governance/privacy in personalization, benchmark saturation and data leakage in continuous evaluation, and immature long-horizon lifelong-learning evaluation.
oracle_or_external_feedback_dependency: n/a (survey) but it makes feedback source an explicit discriminating axis: methods range from intrinsic-only/self-verify (Self-Refine, SPO self-preference, MM-UPT/CoVo self-rewarding RL) through external tool/verifier (compilers, web verifiers, WebRL ORM) to oracle-label/ground-truth and environment-reward. Table 3 classifies each surveyed method's feedback source as internal vs external, surfacing the dependency on external/verifiable signal.
self_correction_efficacy: task-dependent (survey synthesis). It reports that self-evolution yields measurable gains in many settings (in-context improvement accumulates with experience; memory/skill distillation improves repeated/similar tasks) but warns that performance can degrade as benchmarks evolve, that off-policy self-evolution risks reward hacking, and that continual self-modification risks catastrophic forgetting and safety/alignment drift ('misevolution'); efficacy is conditioned on feedback quality and source.
calibration_effect: not-measured (survey does not directly study reasoning-model calibration / 'reasoning tax'). It discusses adaptivity, robustness, and safety as evaluation goals and warns of overconfident drift and misevolution, but does not report calibration metrics.
failure_attribution_capability: classifies-failure-mode (taxonomy-style). The survey itself is a taxonomy/roadmap; it organizes failure-related challenges (catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking, misevolution/safety drift, distribution shift, benchmark saturation/data leakage) and surveys multi-agent and step-level/process-level signal granularity, but does not perform per-step or per-agent counterfactual failure attribution.
failure_mode_addressed: Field-level failure modes it foregrounds: catastrophic forgetting and stability-plasticity dilemma in continual learning; reward hacking / exploitation of train-deploy inconsistencies under off-policy learning; misevolution (safety/alignment/fairness degradation during evolution, per Shao et al. 2025); distribution shift; superficial/ineffective self-reflection without external verification; benchmark saturation and data leakage during continuous evaluation; non-linear compute blow-up. Relates to MAST-style modes such as superficial self-reflection and inter-agent misalignment in multi-agent co-evolution.
dataset_or_benchmark_released: No new dataset proposed by the survey itself; it releases a curated GitHub resource repository (https://github.com/CharlesQ9/Self-Evolving-Agents). It catalogs/recommends emerging benchmarks (MemoryAgentBench TTL, LTMBenchmark, LifelongAgentBench, AUTOENV-36, StuLife, TRACE, Benchmark Self-Evolving) and proposes evaluation protocols/metrics (Cost-per-Gain, BWT/FGT, Personal Adaptation Gain, Data Minimization Score).
builds_on: Synthesizes and is grounded in prior self-improvement / reflection / memory / agent works it surveys, including Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023), Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), STaR / Quiet-STaR (Zelikman et al. 2022/2024), ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2024), Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al. 2024), Voyager-style skill libraries, SEAL/self-edit intra-test-time SFT (Zweiger et al. 2025), WebRL (Qi et al. 2024), DigiRL (Bai et al. 2024), TextGrad, PromptBreeder/APE/ProTeGi/PromptAgent, ADAS, and DPO/RRHF; positioned relative to curriculum learning, lifelong/continual learning, model editing, and unlearning.
extended_by_or_inspired: As a recent (2025/2026) survey it primarily aggregates rather than being extended; it is being cited as a reference roadmap by subsequent self-evolving / continual-learning agent papers and surveys (e.g., works on misevolution safety, ReasoningBank-style memory, agentic context engineering). [uncertain] for specific named direct successors.
citation_count: ~39 (Google Scholar via arXiv/OpenReview listing, mid-2026); Princeton research portal listed ~32 — figure is rising and source-dependent
reasoning_model_native: Partially. The survey covers self-evolution for general LLM agents and explicitly includes RL-emergent reasoning/self-improvement (STaR, test-time RL such as LADDER, R1-style reward-driven adaptation) but is not specific to o1/R1-style native-reflection models; it treats reflection/evolution as orthogonal to whether the base model is a reasoning model.
on_policy_distillation_link: Relevant. The survey discusses on-policy vs off-policy learning as a cross-cutting 'how to evolve' axis, off-policy learning from prior policy versions / experience libraries for sample efficiency (with distribution-shift/reward-hacking caveats), and distillation of reflection/experience into reusable artifacts (skills, workflows, rules, prompts, weights) — directly connecting to on-policy distillation / skill-optimization themes.
sample_efficiency: n/a as a single number (survey). It frames sample efficiency as a design trade-off: off-policy methods improve sample efficiency at the cost of distribution mismatch; intra-test-time methods adapt from as little as a single synthetic example (TT-SI) or focused variant sets (LADDER); proposes Cost-per-Gain / tokens-per-success as efficiency metrics rather than reporting a fixed trial count.
